name: Scarmaxxing

lead: Scarmaxxing is a style meta in which a scar, most often a slit through an eyebrow or a mark on the cheek, is treated as a feature that makes a face look more distinctive, dangerous or experienced. Proponents describe it as a "halo": a single striking detail that shifts how the rest of the face is read.

The idea is discussed mostly as a thought experiment or personal anecdote. Users report more eye contact or curiosity from strangers, while others in the same threads suggest the attention may come from the scar itself rather than overall looks. No studies have tested scarring as a way to raise attractiveness.

paras: Most discussion is about which existing scars to leave untreated or how to present them, with a smaller number of users describing deliberate marks such as an eyebrow slit. Posters note that results depend on skin type and healing, and that placement near nerves matters. Several threads open with disclaimers that the practice should not be attempted.

Scars are permanent. Traditional scarification literature lists infection, bloodborne disease from shared tools, and unwanted keloid or hypertrophic scarring as documented risks, and the outcome varies with skin type and depth. Users also report that a scar can lead to being perceived as low-class or threatening.

lead: Scarmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for treating a scar as a deliberate part of one's look, most often on the face. It covers leaving existing scars untreated as a rugged feature, choosing how to present them, and, in a minority of forum accounts, acquiring a new mark such as an eyebrow slit.[1][2][3]

The appearance chain proponents describe is that a visible scar acts as a "halo": a single striking detail that makes a face more memorable and suggests an eventful past, which in turn changes how the rest of the face is read. Posters report extra eye contact or curiosity from strangers, while others in the same threads suggest the attention is a reaction to the injury and that the mark can also lead to being seen as low-class or threatening.[2][3]

Research on the underlying question exists in two strands. A 2009 study by Rowland, Little and Burriss found that digitally added mild facial scars raised women's ratings of men's attractiveness for short-term, but not long-term, relationships, and that the effect was small.[4][5] A 2022 study from the University of Pennsylvania of 1,800 raters found that a single well-healed facial scar made no significant overall difference to attractiveness ratings.[6] Scarification, the intentional making of scars, is an established practice in many cultures and carries documented infection and scarring risks.[7]

paras: The scarmaxxing idea rests on the belief that a scar changes how a face is perceived, adding a rugged or "dangerous" quality. One forum author frames a scar as something that should "look good, cool" and suggest that something notable happened to the wearer, and notes that people may be curious but others may avoid the wearer.[3] A long guide on looksmax.org discusses scars as a halo, includes examples of people with scars, and opens with repeated disclaimers that nothing in it should be done; replies in that thread question why it was written given the warnings.[1]

In practice the topic has two main forms: keeping and styling scars that already exist (for example from acne, accidents or surgery), and a much less common discussion of deliberately acquiring one. Most threads sit in the first category or treat the second as a thought experiment.

The term sits in the "-maxxing" vocabulary of looksmaxxing forums, where one early thread titled as a method promoted purposely giving yourself a scar as part of a "piratemaxxing" look, with the author adding that results may vary.[3] Later threads on looksmax.org include a first-person account of an eyebrow slit and a long guide on scarification as a halo.[2][1]

The idea echoes older appearance traditions. In Germany and Austria, facial scars from academic fencing (Mensur) duels, known as Schmiss, were regarded as a badge of honour from at least 1825 and were most common among university students in dueling societies around the start of the 20th century. They were thought to signal courage and status and to make a man good husband material, and Otto von Bismarck reportedly admired them.[8] Some people who did not fence imitated the look, with accounts of students cutting themselves with razors or reopening healing wounds.[8] German law allowed honour duels until World War I, the Nazis banned the university Mensur, and the custom faded after World War II, although about 400 fraternities still keep the tradition.[8]

Scarification more broadly is the practice of scratching, etching, burning or cutting designs into the skin so that they heal as scars. It is documented among Indigenous peoples of Africa, Melanesia and Australia, and was historically more visible on darker skin than tattoos.[7] Beyond tradition, the modern body-modification community also includes scarification as a form of body art.[9]

A user who described getting an eyebrow slit reported that women on the street held eye contact longer, and speculated that the effect worked because he already had dark features; he also listed being seen as low-class or criminal, including by police, as a downside.[2] Replies suggested the stares might reflect the visible injury rather than attractiveness, and another described a similar effect from a face tattoo as a "dark triad" cue.[2]

Another poster recommended a straight line on the outer eyebrow, and the original thread author wrote that scars attract curiosity but also avoidance from some people.[3] The long scarification guide presents the topic as discussion and information while stating that it does not recommend scarring for beauty.[1]

Scarification is also called cicatrization. Techniques described in reference sources include rubbing ink or other pigment into a cut, lifting and cutting away skin, and packing a wound with inert material such as clay or ash so that it heals as a raised scar. Outcomes are hard to predict because skin type, cut depth and healing care all matter, and scars tend to spread, so designs are usually kept simple. Healing takes roughly six to twelve months.[7]
Traditional meanings include rites of passage (such as the crocodile-scale marks of Chambri boys in Papua New Guinea), endurance, clan identity, beauty and, among some groups, medicinal beliefs.[7]

The 2009 study in Personality and Individual Differences, by H. M. Rowland, A. Little and R. Burriss, had 147 women and 76 men rate opposite-sex faces that were either unscarred or digitally altered to show realistic mild scarring. Scarring increased women's ratings of men's attractiveness for short-term relationships but not for long-term ones, and did not change men's ratings of women. The authors describe the effect as small and suggest scars may signal useful information under some conditions.[4] Press coverage quoted Burriss as saying that women may see scarring as an attractive quality for short-term relationships and that unscarred men could be seen as more caring and more suitable for long-term relationships; a summary of the work reports scars making men about 6 percent more attractive on average.[5][10] The explanations offered, such as masculinity, bravery or good genes, are the researchers' interpretations rather than tested mechanisms.[5][10]

A 2022 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery by Jesse A. Taylor and colleagues digitally added 14 scars in different locations and orientations to facial photographs; 1,800 respondents produced nearly 89,000 ratings of confidence, friendliness and attractiveness on a 0 to 5 scale. Average attractiveness was 4.25 for scarred faces and 4.26 for unscarred faces, scarred faces were rated friendlier, and a scar on the mid lower eyelid running perpendicular to facial tension lines was rated lower while a parallel one was rated higher. The authors describe the effects as small, at most about 2 percent of the rating.[6]
Both studies used digitally added scars on photographs rather than naturally healed scars in real-life encounters.[4][6]

Scars are permanent. A scar is a normal result of wound repair and is not considered mature until the wound has fully healed, which can take months.[11] Wounds under about 2 mm often heal without scarring, and mechanical tension on a wound can promote scarring.[11]

Reference sources list infection when tools are not sterilised, and bloodborne disease such as HIV and hepatitis C linked to shared tools, as documented risks of scarification.[7] Hypertrophic scars (raised) and keloids (growing beyond the wound edge) are possible; keloids are most common in people with darker skin and in people aged roughly 10 to 30, can be triggered by injuries such as piercings, burns or acne, and recur in roughly 70 to 100 percent of cases when removed by excision alone.[11][12] Forum users add that nerves near the surface of the face can be damaged and that a visible scar may lead to being treated as low-class or criminal.[2][3]

No clinical trials of scarmaxxing or deliberate scarification for appearance have been published. Related research is limited to the perception experiments described above, in which raters judged photographs with digitally added scars.[4][6]

On looksmax.org the topic appears in a handful of threads over several years, some enthusiastic and some framed as hypothetical with health warnings.[1][2][3] It overlaps with other trait-based style metas that rely on a single distinctive feature, such as piratemaxxing or face tattoos.[2][3]

claims.claim: A facial scar acts as a "halo" that makes a face more interesting.
An eyebrow slit draws extra eye contact from women.
Scars signal masculinity, bravery and 'good genes'.
Scars make a man more attractive only for short-term relationships.
Placement matters: a line through the outer eyebrow looks best.
Deliberate scarring can lead to unwanted outcomes.
